13 Billion Years Old Galactic Core Called Dún Aonghasa Has Astronomers Scratching Their Heads
6 photos
Photo: ESA
There are things in this Universe of ours that the average human mind will never be able to properly understand. Like, say, a quasar that existed 13.1 billion years ago and had the mass of no less than 360 million suns.
They call it J1504+6252, or Dún Aonghasa, after the prehistoric cliff-top fort on Inis Mór, in Ireland, and it is, by all intents and purposes, the most distant quasar discovered to date. Spotted by the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope, its light reaches us over the eons from just 630 million years after the Big Bang .
As a reminder, quasars are essentially galactic cores comprising a supermassive black hole, the accretion disk, and jets of energy. As it feeds on the surrounding gas, it releases a tremendous amount of energy, which is what Euclid sees.
Normally, quasars are not forever, and Dún Aonghasa probably turned into a normal galaxy with a black hole at its center a long time ago. The light seen in the images snapped by Euclid has long stopped shining.
The Euclid finding is not important only because it's the most distant quasar ever discovered, but also because it kind of has astronomers scratching their heads at how such an enormous black hole could have existed so close to the Big Bang. There is no answer to that question yet, but the discovery is still young...
The finding announced this week breaks a previous Euclid quasar record, made public a few months back, by no less than 40 million years. It has already been confirmed using a number of other telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble, and the James Webb Space Telescope.
It is because of Webb that we now know the quasar has a black hole with the mass of 360 million suns at its core to power it.
The Euclid telescope launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket back in 2023, and positioned itself at Lagrange Point 2 (L2), 932,000 miles (1.5 million km) from Earth. In the time it has been active, it found 12 new quasars beyond redshift 7 (about 12.9 billion light-years away). The Dún Aonghasa is the only confirmed one beyond redshift 8.
The studies performed so far on the cosmic object point to it having grown extremely rapidly very early in the life of the Universe, and it is considered a rarity of account of the relatively slow rate in consumes material. According to ESA , this puts pressure on models of early black hole formation and growth, and only time will tell if we'll be able to clear up the mess the discovery has generated.
The main mission of the Euclid telescope is to study dark matter and dark energy and how they impact the visible Universe. It will also try to find a reason why its expansion is gaining speed. To do that, it will generate the largest 3D map of the Universe ever created.
Earlier this month, ESA released the first batch of data from the telescope, 1.7 million GB of it. The release, called DR1-Foundation , includes 13 months' worth of observations, and it'll probably keep astronomers busy for ages to come.
